prompt: Review this change before it merges. The change is the last commit of this checkout, a .php project. Get the diff with `git diff 965f1889b05513602624f0e077d3e8534be36c5e HEAD`. Title: Multi steps tasks | AI services integration. Review only this checkout at HEAD. Do not build or run tests. Reply with the full review report.

expected.text: Retry logic is broken. On first failure, both the step (line 113) and parent task (line 124) are immediately marked FAILED, then the exception is re-thrown. On the next retry attempt, the guard at line 54 fires (`step.status === FAILED`) and returns silently — the job is consumed without re-executing the action. The `$tries = 3` setting is effectively `$tries = 1` for actual business logic. Transient failures (network errors, AI API timeouts) will permanently fail tasks with no recovery.

When `TaskActionService::execute` returns `executed: false` (unknown or misconfigured action name), the step is silently marked COMPLETED with `{'status': 'no_action_found'}` instead of FAILED. The pipeline then continues normally and the task eventually reaches COMPLETED. No error is surfaced to the caller, making it impossible to detect mis-spelled or missing action names in task configuration.

`normalise()` accepts any string as `action_name` without validating it against `config/actions.php`. A user posting to `POST /api/v1/tasks` with a multi-step type (e.g., `multi_step_task`) can supply `input.steps[].action_name` with arbitrary values. Combined with the silent no-op in ExecuteTaskStepJob (finding #2), the entire pipeline completes successfully while performing no actual work. The action registry constraint that `RunSingleActionRequest` enforces is absent from the explicit-steps path.

The task is unconditionally marked COMPLETED (line 78) regardless of the action result. If the action returned `status: 'failed'` in its result array (e.g., `ScrapeUrlAction` with an invalid URL, `AskAiAction` with no prompt), the task is still marked COMPLETED. Callers polling `GET /api/v1/tasks/{id}` receive `status: completed` with a failed action result buried in `meta_json.action_result`, creating a misleading contract.

`$e->getMessage()` is returned directly in the API-visible `error` field. Exception messages from Laravel's HTTP client (connection refused, redirect to disallowed URL, SSL errors) can expose internal hostnames, IP addresses, or infrastructure details. The redirect callback at line 36 explicitly includes the disallowed URI in its exception message, which then surfaces to the caller. Error messages should be sanitised or mapped to generic user-facing strings.

`resolve()` instantiates concrete service classes directly via `app(OpenAIService::class)` etc., bypassing the DI binding registered in `AppServiceProvider`. If a developer rebinds `OpenAIService` in the container (e.g., for testing or to swap an implementation), `AIServiceResolver` will ignore it and construct the original class. The provider selection logic is now duplicated between `AppServiceProvider` and `AIServiceResolver`, creating a maintenance trap where adding a new provider requires changes in two places.

The `isAllowedUrl` check has a potential Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability due to a Time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition. The `isPublicHost` method checks the DNS record of the host, but the actual HTTP request is made later. An attacker could point a domain to a public IP during the check, and then switch it to a private IP before the HTTP client makes the request. The comment correctly identifies this risk but it remains a significant vulnerability.

This test (and `test_pipeline_honours_explicit_steps_in_input_json` if it included scrape) runs the full multi-step pipeline against the `scrape_and_summarize` task type. The default plan invokes `ScrapeUrlAction`, which performs a real outbound HTTP request (`Http::get(...)`) and a real DNS lookup (`dns_get_record(...)`) against `https://example.com`. There is no `Http::fake()` / DNS stub set up here, so this test depends on the CI/dev environment having network access and on `example.com` being reachable, making it flaky and slow. Consider faking the HTTP client (`Http::fake([...])`) or injecting/mocking `ScrapeUrlAction` for these tests so the suite remains hermetic.

The set of "multi-step" task types is hard-coded here and again in `TaskPlannerService::defaultPlan()`. Adding a new multi-step task type requires touching at least two unrelated places (and they can drift silently — e.g. a type added only to the planner would still be routed through the legacy `LogTaskRequestJob` path here, while a type added only here would dispatch the plan job but produce the default no-op `save_result` step). Consider centralizing this list (for example, in a config file or in `TaskPlannerService`) and consuming it from the controller, so the contract between routing and planning stays in sync.

The retry guard in `PlanTaskStepsJob` relies on a prior `pluck()` and this non-unique index, so two planner jobs for the same task can both observe no existing step and insert duplicate `(task_id, sequence_order)` rows. Add a unique constraint (and use an atomic upsert/firstOrCreate keyed by it) to make retries and duplicate dispatches safe under concurrency.

Step claiming is a non-atomic read-then-update. If the same `ExecuteTaskStepJob` is delivered twice concurrently, both workers can read `pending` before either save, then both run the action; side effects like AI calls or `save_result` writes can happen twice. Claim the row with an atomic conditional update/lock before executing the action.

This check-then-insert retry guard is not atomic. If duplicate planner jobs run concurrently for the same task, both can read the same `$existingOrders` and create duplicate steps because the database does not enforce uniqueness on `(task_id, sequence_order)`. This should use a database-backed unique key with `upsert`/`firstOrCreate` semantics.

This worker command uses `ai-agent:service` and `ai-agent:task`, but jobs are dispatched to `QueueEnum::SERVICE`/`QueueEnum::TASK`, which resolve to `service` and `task`, and the supervisor docs use those same names. Following this command would leave the new pipeline jobs unprocessed.

`AskAiAction` always returns `status: ok` after `chat()` even when the resolved provider response contains no extractable answer text. The bundled Ollama/Anthropic stubs return `status: not_configured` and no `choices`, so `ask_ai` reports success with an empty `text`, and pipeline tasks can complete as if an AI answer was generated.

The scraper reads the entire response body into memory before truncating it to 5,000 characters. A user-controlled URL can return a very large response and exhaust worker memory despite the 12-second timeout. Add a response size limit/streaming read or reject responses over a configured maximum before loading the whole body.
